To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the induction of HO in spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR) lowers blood pressure (BP) by increasing the production of carbon monoxide (CO).
hemin treatment of SHR for 3 weeks induced HO-1, reduced blood pressure, and prevented hypertension in SHR offspring.
the HO inhibitor tin protoporphyrin (SnPP) attenuated the development of hypertension, and hemin reversed established hypertension, in the SHR.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of heme oxygenases (HOs) in the regulation of vascular tone.
the role of heme oxygenases (HO) and their metabolites in cardiovascular diseases.
the regulation of the enzyme heme-oxygenase (HO) in the kidney, and with its possible role as a regulator of renal function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hemin, a substrate for and inducer of HO–CO, is a potent antihypertensive agent in SHR.
HO induction is a potentially important therapeutic strategy in the management of hypertension.
hemin administration in the SHR induces HO and CO, which in turn induces cGMP, which leads to vasodilation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have found that hemin is a very potent antihypertensive compound in the SHR.

we have found that HO–CO is a vasodilator and a regulator of vascular tone and that this may be an important pathway in the regulation of blood pressure and the pathophysiology of hypertension.5,6,7 The first question is whether hemin is a substrate or an inducer of heme oxygenases.

HO and CO are not only involved in the regulation of vascular tone but also in a number of other physiological functions, including the modulation of inflammatory processes, cell proliferation and differentiation, angiogenesis, and apoptosis.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the HO–CO system is an integral part of the vascular control mechanism.5 The vasodilator effects of CO are mediated by the cGMP-dependent protein kinase G,6 and this system may be an important part of the vascular response to hypoxia.7 However, the vasodilation is not as robust as that of NO, and it has been difficult to demonstrate the presence of CO as an endothelium-derived vasodilator, although this has been reported in some studies

the HO–CO–cGMP pathway is a potent regulator of vascular function.5,6 We have also shown that HO-1, the inducible isoform of HO, is a major determinant of blood pressure in SHR,7 and that HO activity and CO production are elevated in the SHR kidney.8 However, we have not previously reported a blood pressure–lowering effect of hemin.
HO is a major determinant of blood pressure in this model of hypertension and that its induction can reverse hypertension in the SHR, but it also raises many questions.
